records.title: Show HN: RDST – A local agent that watches Postgres/MySQL for query regressions
records.author: gvsg
records.storyText:
We noticed during the course of many many years of DBA related work that fixes to database issues and queries are always reactive. An entire database can fall over extremely quickly when an unbounded query grows without warning.

Traditionally, DBAs hear complaints of slowness and follow a methodical process: - manually browse pg_stats or other database related performance internal tables - see which queries are slowest - figure out what indexes are missing - figure out which indexes are actually bad and slowing down writes - painstakingly implement a fix

In the age of cheap intelligence, we decided that there is no reason we can’t have an always-on agent that is designed to do this job for you. Databases need something or someone that is always watching with a massive amount of contextual understanding to be able to take quick actions. We’ve watched the alternative play out repeatedly. One of our users’s checkout page went from loading instantly to taking 11 seconds in a single night with no code change. How? Well somehow their order table grew by 40M rows because BI team had injected historical data and suddenly postgres started doing full table scans. Sometimes routine operations have unintended results and can easily destroy your database. We wanted to catch these kinds of regressions instantly. So we built RDST.

RDST is a desktop agent that runs on your PC and connects to PostgreSQL / MYSQL (read only) and compares every query against its own performance every minute. Every expensive query is automatically EXPLAIN ANALYZED, stripped of PII and sent to U.S. based frontier or open model providers to analyze which indexes are missing, how the query could be rewritten, and provides the fix. We then run a classifier model (JEV) to decide if you should be notified (is this standard behavior for this particular query?), and the full history of the query performance is kept for years. RDST also keeps track of your entire database health in general, and recommends more fixes than simply bad queries.

Since it runs locally we can keep the database credentials stored in your OS Keychain (RDST never keeps them in its own storage layer), and the connection goes straight to your database (using a jump host or SSH tunnel for private connections). You can read more about how we handle data especially as it pertains to LLM use here.

https://readyset.io/docs/readyset-ai/rdst/desktop/privacy

We really want feedback from the community from people running Postgres and MySQL in production. We are giving inference away completely for free.

Just as a reminder, RDST will NOT run any updates or indexes against your database at this time. We are considering a fully autonomous auto-pilot mode in the future, but for now we are leaving the actual fixes in your hands.

Let us know what you think!

records.title: Show HN: Endo – A Higher-Order Harness
records.author: Warren93
records.storyText:
Endo is a Higher-Order Harness (HOH).

From the easiest concept to understand to the more complex ones, Endo gives you: * A single, simple UI to use any agent provider with your existing subscriptions, and hot-swap agents right in the middle of a session. * An orchestration layer, which I call HOH, allowing arbitrary composition of agents to achieve any workflow. A fun case I tried was asking Fable and Astra to mock a presidential debate. * An agent protocol that abstracts any agent. The key insight here is that every LLM is an agent—instead of treating the LLM as just one node inside an external ReAct loop.

Endo was a concept formed while I was building OpenChart (https://github.com/longsurf-ai/openchart). To power trading workflows, I needed to support scenarios where strict determinism is required, while still keeping the flexibility of an agent's inference-time decision-making capability. A new form factor was needed between rigid n8n-style workflows and open-ended ReAct loop agents.

Thus the creation of Endo. Endo is short for Endomorphism, a term rooted in category theory and functional programming. An endomorphism is a function that transforms an object into another object of the same type. Similarly, Endo itself is built purely on functional programming principles, relying heavily on Effect (https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect).

..And if you have patience to speak technical jargons, Endo is: * An agent orchestration layer—Higher-Order Harness (HOH)—where an entire agent is treated the same as a single LLM call, enabling arbitrary composition of extremely complex workflows. * A way to abstract any harness into a standardized protocol, where raw models and agents behave the exact same way, in a KV-cache-friendly manner. * A workflow engine that enables arbitrary composition of agents with a single workflow language.

It's completely open source, and if you think this idea is cool, let's build together. Just for the fun of it.

records.title: Show HN: Videre – a Rust CLI to manage your photos and videos with joy
records.author: erhangundogan
records.storyText:
Long story short it's a media library licensed under Apache2. It cares about your privacy. It doesn't send any data and it doesn't have telemetry. It is local only project. It' helps you to organize, view, search and do plenty of things with your photos and videos locally. If you are interested in it's story you can read on OR visit https://videre.sh for installation instructions.

I have been collecting my photos and videos since 2000s. My collection grew exponentially when I bought iPhone 3GS back in 2010. I had roughly 1TB of backups in multiple iPhoto folders. It was nice at the beginning but than I realized that there are multiple copies of files in multiple backups. It's not just one or two, they were like thousands because I copied them here and there time to time from drive to external drive and import from iCloud etc.

So There was a big chunk of unnecessary data sitting in my external drive. I tried iPhoto itself to resolve it but it wasn't good enough. So I decided to write small app (dedupe) to eliminate them by myself. The story of `videre` started like that. There is a longer story in videre.sh/blog if you would like to read.

`videre` is local & privacy first CLI tool. You can do many things with it such as duplicate elimination, date/time fix with EXIF/mtime support, recognise/cluster faces automatically, date grouping, event detection, map, advanced search via composable filters and lucene syntax, import/export Google/Apple/Adobe, XMP support, tags/keywords etc. Other media libraries have similar features but the difference of `videre` is CLI. Since it runs in terminal it's very convenient to use it via AI Assistant. So you don't even have to know all those commands and their usages. You may ask to you AI assistant: "Find my photos with George in NY at last summer by using videre" and that should be enough (of course you need to define who is George via `videre gallery` People section first).

I enjoy using it. It's not because I built, it's a strong tool and you can do many things. Especially it's gallery command and web UI is strongly recommended. I bet all of you need such tool at some point so just give it a shot. Installation is very easy and then scan some files and see `videre gallery` UI/UX. Hope you enjoy it.

Github: https://github.com/aegea-dev/videre Docs: https://docs.videre.sh

records.title: Show HN: Weatheristic.com to answer questions other weather sites don't
records.author: zievo
records.storyText:
I built this for myself. I often have questions I want quick answers to such as "how cold did it get last night?", "I just put down fertilizer, when will it rain next?", "is today unusually cold or warm for this time of year?" Weather sites I tried made me dig for those answers, if they were there at all (the last few days of weather often can't be found).

I used to watch a few stocks closely, and Weatheristic is actually inspired by those types of charts. It has day/night bands with an ultra easy to understand temp trend line, and you can zoom and scroll. I added data I'm interested in, such as a typical high/low band, record high/low for today, moon phases, and various other items in the Overlays dropdown.

One deliberate choice: the temperature scale doesn’t rescale. It stays at roughly -4F to 86F (−20C to 30C) most of the time, so the line’s height on the y-axis tells you how warm it is before you read a number. So if the graph seems off center to you, that's by design.

Data comes from Open-Meteo. The historical records come from their reanalysis archive, which is modelled data rather than weather-station readings, so daily extremes might be a bit off. It’s a static D3 site. No account, no ads, no cookies. I count visits with self-hosted Plausible (cookieless, no personal data; it lives at analytics.povodex.com because I run it for my other projects too).

I use this every day, love it, and I’d love to know if anyone else likes this format.

records.title: Show HN: CoolDock – a second Dock for macOS with live widgets and an MCP server
records.author: pugdogdev
records.storyText:
I always hated desktop widgets because I never see them. They sit behind every window I have open. Same problem with Notification Center, it's hidden away so I never use it.

The dock, however, is always there, it's already taking the real estate from the bottom of my screen, so why not add a second dock on the exact same real estate, that shows up as soon as the dock hides and vice versa, but not for apps - for widgets!

CoolDock is that solution with 20+ widget categories - music, weather, AI usage, 3rd party integrations, mail, todo, habit tracker, posture reminder, water reminder and over 150 wallpapers to switch to based on my mood.

And the best part is that it looks completely native with Liquid Glass, doesn't require disabling the macOS default dock and runs completely local, no telemetry, no account, only widgets and your integrations. Oh and best part #2 - I added an MCP server so I don't actually have to clickops my way to complete setup, I could just ask my AI to add a widget and configure it however I want it (MCP starts as read-only, you can choose to give it permission to actually change things).

I actually acquired CoolDock from its original developer, and it's the second dock app I acquired from a developer (ExtraDock was the first). CoolDock currently has passed 1,200 users

I am constantly adding new widgets based on user requests, currently at 160+ widgets to choose from, you can see them on the website https://cooldock.app

Happy to answer any question!

records.title: Show HN: Cr34te.it – a website anyone can rewrite one turn at a time with AI
records.author: y42
records.storyText:
Yeah I built this out of a silly idea a couple of weeks ago.

You can change what the website shows. You may change minor things or add something completely new. It bascially works like that:

1. You claim a turn. If the queue is empty, you start right away.

2. When it's your turn, you copy a prompt to a web based AI or - more comfy - our local coding agent.

3. The AI will fetch the current status of the website and ask what you want to change.

4. You answer - and the AI gets back a JSON that you paste back to the website - or the coding agent POST it directly to an endpoint.

5. Submission will be moderated against all of the things you must expect when anonymous people post stuff. There are a couple of apparenty restrictions. You will find out.

6. Eventually it's being published.

Historical submissions are being preserved, you can browse them.

records.title: Show HN: Turbo Lisp – A Common Lisp IDE for macOS and the Terminal
records.author: stray
records.storyText:
When Apple left Clozure Common Lisp behind by switching to Apple Silicon, I started kicking around the idea of building my own Lisp/Objective-C bridge by combining Apple Documentation, the clang AST, and introspection of the Objective-C runtime.

There was a CCL porting effort, but I really wanted to use SBCL anyway.

Truth be told — what I really wanted was a 21st-century CLIM variant on top of modern AppKit 26. So I let that idea rattle around in my skull for a while — and eventually it bounced up against the memory of Ck (Curses-based Tk).

Anybody remember that?

I liked Tcl/Tk and [incr Tcl] and it had always stuck in my head how great an idea it was to have something along the lines of CLIM for regular terminals as well as GUI.

So anyway, I stumbled upon the open-source CLIM2 source still maintained by Franz, and the wheels commenced to turn.

Oh yeah, and my very first programming environment had been Turbo Pascal. That integrated debugger was really something.

And y'know, it all started to come together as an idea about modernizing CLIM and modifying Portable Hemlock to run on top of it — and integrating a Debugger with conditional breakpoints and Step In/Step Out/Step Over, CLIM presentations, Inspector...

And in years past, I'd have just dreamed about it.

But the past three years have been crazy. GPT4 was the first time I seriously tried to build things with an LLM. And I've been pushing the LLMs as far as they would go to build my intuition mainly.

But up until this year they've been mostly crap.

I used "Build Common Lisp" as my north star because the Dietz ANSI tests seemed like a nearly perfect product specification.

Long story short: I threw away 7 attempts before I won ANSI — https://gitlab.com/patchwork1-ai/whateverlisp — and while I was waiting for Claude and Codex to grovel through ANSI I was trying my hand at my grand idea of Turbo Lisp.

Side note: my high score on ANSI is 21,916/21,925 passing (99.96%); 21,925 executed; 9 failing. And those 9? Yeah I don't think you could pass those without failing 30+ other ones.

So anyway — It’s called *Turbo Lisp* (based on SBCL). It brings together a Listener, debugger, object inspector, conditional breakpoints + stepper, and Zeta—a variant of Portable Hemlock that uses WhateverCLIM as its front-end.

On macOS, it uses native AppKit UI through *Chattanooga, a Lisp/Objective-C bridge I built*. It also runs in the terminal through *Oak Ridge, my Lisp port of Ratatui*. Both use *WhateverCLIM*, which is the CLIM2 code from Franz plus my own modernization, including *presentations*: displayed Lisp objects you can click and inspect.

*v0.2.1 patch release* is available for Apple Silicon Macs, Intel Macs, and Linux x86-64. The Mac builds currently require macOS 26.

I’m especially interested in hearing:

* Does it install and start properly on your machine? * Can you find your way around the Listener, editor, and debugger? * Does the terminal interface work with your terminal emulator? * Where does it feel confusing, awkward, or broken?

A report that says “I tried this and got stuck here” is useful. Please include your OS, CPU architecture, and terminal emulator where relevant.

It’s still early, and I’m looking for honest feedback from people using it outside my own setup.

records.title: Show HN: Sufuku – Sudoku, but Numbers Repeat
records.author: matthorse
records.storyText:
Sudoku is short for "the digits must be single". I wondered if inverting this would work: "the digits must be repeated". And so, by swapping "doku" for "fuku", Sufuku was born.

In short, instead of using numbers 1-9 for a 9x9 board, you use 2 twice, 3 three times, and 4 four times (for a total of 9).

It plays differently from sudoku than I expected. I assumed it would be simpler, since you have fewer digits. But once I settled on irregular region shapes, I discovered that it can also be quite difficult. In sudoku you eliminate a number by placing it; in sufuku a number is only eliminated once all its copies are placed. So you count lines instead of mostly scanning the board.

As I want the game to be approachable, the daily boards are mostly 6x6 or 7x7 for now. Larger boards are more interesting because 6x6 has only one set of numbers: [1, 2, 3]. But for 9x9 you can go with [2, 3, 4], [1, 3, 5], or [1, 2, 6] (I skip pairs like [2, 7] because I consider them boring). 10x10 is the first one that offers a set of four numbers: [1, 2, 3, 4].

Of course it turns out the idea has been around for some time: 2-3-4 Sudoku (Uwe Wiedemann) and Sudoku Ripeto (Miguel Palomo). I'm curious what you make of it as a daily game.

Today's Friday, so the board is on the harder side. You can play easier boards in this week's archive.

records.author: beardnetworks

Hi HN Folks,

I have been building Kitaphone a web app that lets you call regular mobile and landline numbers directly from your browser. The idea is simple, there are still plenty of situations where apps like WhatsApp, facetime and other internet calling apps aren't an option. For example, when you are abroad and need to call your bank, an airline, or a government office or your son/daughter's school.

I wanted to make those calls possible without requiring users to install another app or buy a sim card or even commit to a monthly subscription. I built Kitaphone using Next.js and Twilio, One of the more interesting challenges has been making browser based calling reliable, especially when it comes to dealing with microphone permissions, sending keypad inputs to automated phone systems, and preventing abuse of free calling credits.

The product is live and supports international calls to regular phone numbers, users currently need an account to make calls partly because each call has a real telecom cost. I am still improving it and learning from the people using it by receiving feedback.

Fun fact: "kita" means our in Bahasa Malaysia, since I am based in this beautiful country and their people are so warm and welcoming I was truly inspired by this place and decided to name it our phone.

Interested to know or receive feedback from HN folks who worked with WebRTC or VoiP in the past.

records.title: Show HN: Tennis, a local/offline context store
records.author: pizzuh
records.storyText:
Hi everyone! I'm Joe, and I built Tennis: a CLI that indexes and searches your context offline. You can index any files, your Chat & Claude sessions, Codex history, etc. All local and offline.

I've always hated having chats siloed in Claude and not having an easy way to connect that context in other apps. Anything that exists today has a subscription and is stored on their servers, and really wanted something fast, local, and offline.

How Tennis works: * SQLite/FTS5 (keyword) + vec0 (vector) * model2vec / potion-retrieval-32M (512-dim, 123MB). This is a flat vector table, and what helps make this work well local/offline. * RRF (k=60) fuses BM25 keyword rank + cosine semantic rank into one score

Tennis also creates markdown files called 'cards' at indexing time. This gives you an easy, summarized, human readable format to see what Tennis has. You can edit these files (but won't change the embeddings in SQLite).

You can use Tennis via API and MCP. It's incredibly fast, and the MCP works great as a connector to different applications (ChatGPT, Claude, Opencode, etc).

You can install and use it today: https://tennis.jlachance1.workers.dev/

Thanks for checking this out! I would love any feedback. Thank you

records.title: Show HN: Monitoring my 'dumb' boiler with AI
records.author: verelo
records.storyText:
I have this boiler at a rental property I own. It has 3 smart thermostats (Ecobee). They're great and give the individual tenants zone control, but they only notify me something is wrong when it's already too late as they rely on observing the 'call for heat' and a ongoing decline in room temperature to trigger the alert.

The boiler is pretty smart, it has all kinds of cool error codes, but the issue is I have no way of knowing theres an error flashing on the screen. That is, until now.

I put a Tapo camera pointed at the boiler (getting Tapo to export still frames was a whole other issue, code for doing that is in the same github project for anyone interested) and use AI to read the screen and zone controller lights.

The result is a system that sends me a text message any time something goes outside of the normal operating parameters. My goal is to deliver a great experience for the tenants living at this property, and now I'm able to connect my 'dumb' appliances to the internet without any of the typical risks associated with exposing critical infrastructure to the web.

records.title: Show HN: Trustmux – Async tmux from your phone, now in Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora
records.author: dustinkirkland
records.storyText:
I'm Dustin Kirkland, author of Byobu. I recently flew to Australia and kept nudging my Claude, Codex, and Bash jobs along back home from somewhere over the Pacific, at 700ms of latency.

That's what Trustmux is for: secure, asynchronous access to your tmux or Byobu sessions from your phone.

I first posted this in June and since then there have been many point releases, lots of new features and testing, and a growing base of users. It's now packaged in Ubuntu 26.10, Debian, Fedora, and Chainguard OS.

Why not SSH, Mosh, or Claude Mobile?

- SSH/Mosh: a live, synchronous connection is brutal on a phone. Latency and WiFi-to-cellular handoffs make it laggy and fragile. - Claude Mobile: great for Claude, but I wanted access to whatever is running in my tmux session: shells, Claude, other code assistants.

Trustmux is async by design. Connect, look, type a command, disconnect, with no fragile connection state to babysit.

Security: TLS with real certificates, end to end. Uses Tailscale (cert provisioning via tailscale serve, no port forwarding) optionally, bind to your own network address, or bring your own or self-signed certs. Two security experts reviewed the design and I implemented their recommendations. More scrutiny is very welcome.

Quick start:

  trustmux enable
  trustmux start
  trustmux pair   # shows a QR code if qrencode is installed
Open the URL on your phone, enter the 6-digit code, and add it to your home screen. It's a PWA, so there's no app store.

Install: apt, dnf, pip install trustmux, or brew tap dustinkirkland/trustmux && brew install trustmux

Under the hood: Python, libtmux, WebSockets, Tailscale, and no polling. The UI shell is cached for offline use. Part of Byobu, GPLv3. Trustmux isn't affiliated with the tmux project.

https://trustmux.dev https://github.com/dustinkirkland/byobu https://pypi.org/project/trustmux/

records.title: Show HN: Beeline Multiplayer Agent Harness
records.author: lunchboxfortwo
records.storyText:
Shipped Beeline today. It's a team chat for humans and agents - a kind of multiplayer harness. You can bring your codex, Claude code, opencode subscriptions and also works with pi and goose. We built beeline itself with early versions of beeline, and use it to build our other projects - it's boosted productivity quite a bit for us.

Demo video: https://youtu.be/ACdelpZC2z4?is=pP6MFxJODvKcGjQt

The key insight is that humans do their best work in teams, but agentic development has so far been single player. This has led to people having to forward AI slop to each other or to try to deliver context through various shims like meetings or task tickets.

Beeline is a single control plane for your entire team, both human and agent, and is designed to help your team do its best work.

Things to expect: - This is a multiplayer agentic harness, not a slack substitute. It's best for focused product teams doing or relying on engineering tools and shipping code. - Open source and not a business. We use beeline internally, and just thought it would be a really cool thing to exist in the world. There are still lots of bugs - Sweepstakes things like computer use, lots of third party connector integrations are there. What's cool is that beeline agents can automate _auth_ through trustysquire.ai - they can sign up to most services and APIs without you having to do it for them. - A new primitive called workflows, that are skills for teams of agents. - multi way call with your entire team, humans and agents. I like it quite a bit.

Looking forward to feedback!

records.title: Show HN: Luksmith – Mount LUKS Ext4 Drives Natively in Finder on Apple Silicon
records.author: baytizzel
records.storyText:
I’ve recently moved over to macOS this summer and previously I heavily used Linux (still do as I have a homeserver running Arch and Omarchy Thinkpad for fun). I have a few LUKS Encrypted hard drives with photos I wanted on my Mac and then quickly realized that there’s no native way to open the drive.

So I spent some time to make luksmith, essentially decrypting the luks drive, mounting the underlying EXT4 drive and using Apple’s Userland FSKit Library to make it appear in the finder window to make it as close to home on a Mac as I can (with journaling caveats because I can’t control which order writes happen in).

It’s completely free to read and copy files from the drive if you try it out ‘brew install --cask betizzel/luksmith/luksmac’. And $9.99 one time purchase to unlock writing to the drive. No account needed, no telemetry shared back to me, no network connections made.

Requires Apple Silicon + macOS 26. Full format support and limitations here: [https://luksmith.app/#formats](https://luksmith.app/#formats)

available on the appstore: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/luksmith/id6806869711?mt=12

records.title: Show HN: Forwarder.cc – Static-site forms sent to your inbox, pay per message
records.author: calyhre
records.storyText:
TL;DR: 12 years ago I built a service that forwards simple HTML forms to an email address. I've been procrastinating on finishing it ever since, until today. You point your form at it and every submission lands in your inbox. It runs on credits, 1 credit = 1 message, no subscription. Perfect for static websites.

—

Hey folks, back around 2014, alongside my job as a software engineer, I was building a lot of static websites for my own clients, mostly small businesses that just wanted a simple site. To avoid headaches, I went fully static, often hosted on GitHub Pages and similar.

But most clients also wanted a contact form, and a form needs a server running somewhere. I had my own weekend-hacked service for this, which literally just forwarded the form to the client's email.

I didn't invent anything here: one service I particularly remember was FormKeep by thoughtbot, that I really liked.

So I started building my own, mostly because I loved losing myself in side projects like this, and also because I was a cheap ass and thought I could do something similar for less, and without a subscription.

By 2016 I had done about 90% of what I'm showing you today. I called it "The Great Forwarder". Everything was ready: backend, frontend, hosting, Stripe, landing page. I even had a designer friend help with the design (sorry, Valentin, if I've botched it since). Then I started another project, which took off right away and took all my attention for a while. Fun fact: that project has been using this service ever since, and almost every message ever sent through it came from there.

So for years, I kept Forwarder.cc up to date, upgrading libraries and trying new ones: axios, got, Redux, Zustand, create-react-app, webpack, Vite… It became my laboratory for everything I wanted to explore, while always staying up and maintained (again, for my own use only).

The only thing that ever held me back from launching it was a missing help center, and, more honestly, the fear of putting it in front of people.

So today's the day: after 12 years of procrastination, I finally finished the help center.

I know there are a ton of similar services nowadays, but anyway, what do you think of that help center?

records.title: Show HN: OutClocked, a nearly impossible daily trivia game
records.author: karolgajda
records.storyText:
I really wanted to use an em dash in that title, but now I feel like I can't.

This is a time-based trivia game with a bit of a twist. 7 questions. 60 seconds to answer the first. 0.94 seconds to answer the last. If you get any question wrong or let the timer expire you're out for that game.

Let's also get this out of the way: I used Claude Code to build this game. The first version took a couple of hours and in total I've spent about 10 hours tweaking and improving it. Happy to talk about that!

The stack is simple: one Cloudflare Worker and D1 (SQLite), plain JS, no framework

If you're a Soundgarden fan you already know what inspired the name of the game, the song Outshined.

What inspired me to create the game is I love trivia (even though I'm not great at it) and a friend of mine built a nearly impossible game completely different to this. That got me thinking what kind of nearly impossible trivia game I could make.

So far 92% of players fail, which makes me think I should make question #7 more difficult because 8% are getting all 7 questions correct.

Totals since launch (not including my own playing/testing):

- 651 games played - 178 (26%) out on the first question - 54 (8%) got 7/7 correct

I've had feedback that has run the gamut from "I hate time games" to "This is so fun!" so I don't even know what to think about feedback anymore. Happy to hear yours!

records.title: Show HN: Agent Chat in Your Markdown Notes – Chat with Context and Save Response
records.author: gb2d_hn
records.storyText:
EtherPK now has Agent Chat.

I use AI agents in two distinct ways. For coding I use TUIs, but for day-to-day and non code projects I used to use the web chat UIs like many others. Two things about this was always jarring:

You're starting context from scratch. You might have a couple of agent instructions configured, but you have to tell the agent what you're thinking, from the beginning. When you get the information you need, holding on to it is hard. Within a day or two it's burried in your chat history. EtherPK is a mardown based PKMS (notes app), and it solves both of these problems.

You can type /Agent within your notes (EtherPK supports standard prose and outliner blocks in the same document). The Agent Chat panel opens within your document, and you can choose how much context to give it. That might be nothing, the current block tree, the document or the whole graph (in the case of the latter - immediate surounding context is sent and the agent is given tools to navigate the rest of your graph). You control what the agent gets, and what stays private.

records.title: Show HN: Pull Presence – See who else is reviewing a GitHub pull request, live
records.author: alexfu914
records.storyText:
Pull Presence is a Chrome extension that gives you visibility into who else may be reviewing a GitHub pull request in real time.

Why? Not sure if anyone else encounters this but I have a few times when I pinged someone asking for a review and then they mentioned they are already reviewing it. I thought to myself, "wouldn't it be neat to see who is currently reviewing?". Also as a reviewer, I think it would be nice for the author to know that I'm currently reviewing. Not sure if this resonates with anyone else.

The way it works is, once you install the extension, you'll need to sign in to GitHub. Then, whenever you open a pull request, the extension connects to a live room for that PR over a websocket. You’ll see who else is viewing it, and when someone goes idle (no activity, or they switched tabs) or leaves. And due to the nature of it, you can only see others that also have the extension installed.

I think it's kinda neat (maybe i'm just biased) but feel free to let me know what you think.

records.storyText: As a current student at UC Berkeley, I mostly have been leveraging AI as a tutor to get me through my classes. As a result, I have a collection of artifacts and tools that primarily help interact with and visualize complex concepts. I've turned this into a side project in the hopes some other people would find this helpful as well. As a broke college student I understand the need behind free educational resources, so this is completely free and will stay free. Looking for feedback, let me know what you think!

records.title: Show HN: Relay – A Mac app that adds /relay command to Claude, Codex and Cursor
records.author: kenn
records.storyText:
Simply put, Relay is just a copy-paster between Claude, Codex and Cursor. It adds a /relay command to those GUIs that just sends the chat history since last over to the other side.

I’ve been working on this small Mac app called Kanary that offers essential features. While building it, I found myself stupidly repeating the process of being a messenger between Claude and Codex.

Then I thought, why not build a feature that helps my development process? What if Kanary could be a meta-app that bridges between harnesses? That’s when I hit on the idea of a meta harness. A wrapper that works IN the GUI apps that we already use, not a new app.

It’s still just a copy-paster, but it has changed how I work tremendously. So far it’s a painkiller for me, not a vitamin. I’d love to hear what you think of this simple tool that does this one simple thing.

75 free relays per week. Copy is always free.

records.title: Show HN: A minimalistic building blocks style C++ coroutine library
records.author: parkovski
records.storyText:
I wrote this originally to use with a sudo for Windows project I'm working on. It's bring-your-own-executor - you can see how I use it with Windows IO completion ports at [1]. The library itself breaks coroutines down into small pieces that can be combined to make many different kinds of tasks and generators - see how they're put together at [2]. Feel free to ask me about C++ coroutines or give feedback.

[1] https://github.com/parkovski/wsudo/blob/master/lib/common/co...

[2] https://github.com/parkovski/wscoro/blob/master/include/wsco...
